newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Disappearing miles.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS: Disappearing miles.

text.p: It's time for frequent fliers to check the fine print. By one estmate 50 billion frequent flier miles in accounts worldwide will expire at the end of this year because travelers haven't claimed them.
The figure comes from Randy Peterson, the Colorado Springs-based mileage wizard who has made a career out of unlocking puzzles often built into frequent flier programmes.
"There are a ton of miles out there. About 37 million people in the United States alone are in mileage programmes," he said.
Many of them pile up mileage credit from telephone cards, credit cards, hotel stays, floral purchases and other sources but never accumulate enough for a free travel award, Peterson said.

That helps account for some of the 50 billion miles that will be erased if not claimed at the end of calendar 1996, he said, along with the fact some of the largest programmes -- incuding the biggest, American Airlines -- have expirations kicking in. It also marks the first time that some miles earned in AT&T's "True Rewards" promotion will be self-destructing.
Peterson advises those who may be within reach of an award certificate to consider options for adding credit before the end of the year, such as making purchases with affinity credit cards.

Peterson points out that travelers can still use the miles after the deadline, provided they've converted them into flight coupons which are in turn good for an extended period of time. But the option must be exercised by year's end.
Peterson says members of mileage programmes or other credit programmes with the following carriers, cards or hotels are not safe from expiring miles, either at year's end or later in 1997:

Aer Lingus, Aeromexico, Air France, ANA, America West, American, Ansett Australia, AT&T, British Airways, British Midland, BWIA, China, El Al, EVA, Finnair, Japan Airlines, KLM, LatinPass, Lufthansa, Mexicana, Northwest, Passages, Qantas, SAS, SAA, Southwest, Swissair/Austrian, Thai, United, Virgin Atlantic, Howard Johnson and Westin.
It is also possible in some programmes to donate miles. American, for example, allows donations in 5,000-mile increments, which it matches one-for-three, and gives to certain charities.

Airlines, incidentally, sell their mileage credit for about two cents a mile to those who give it to their customers. So a car rental company that offers its customers 500 miles for doing business is spending $10 to do it.

Peterson says there a number of emerging programmes which allow mileage programme members to book flights by combing money and mileage credit. He said his operation will be offering a fax service soon which will alert people to such offers by city.

A complete rundwn on expiring miles and other information can be found on Peterson's WebFlyer Internet site -- http://www.insideflyer.com -- and more information about his publications and services can be obtained at 1-800-333-5937
Peterson's Internet site was recently named one of the top 10 for travelers by Omaha, Neb.-based Travel and Transport, one of the country's biggest travel firms.
The other nine it singled out were:

A restaurant locator at www.dinersgrapevine.com, interactive business travel information at www.biztravel.com, worldwide information on cities at www.city.net, maps and specific hotel locations worldwide at www.mapquest.com, airline on-time performance and other information from the U.S. government at www.bts.gov, information on worldwide destinations at www.lonelyplanet.com, latest weather including 30-minute radar updates at www.weather.com, information from Fodor's travel at www.fodors.com and currency conversion information at www.mastercard.com.
